blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A team writes its planner memo by copying numbers from a solver's console, and its finance memo from a spreadsheet export of the same run. What should change?

options.text: Nothing, since two memos about the same run always carry the same numbers
options.says: Copied numbers drift: a typo or a stale export puts different values in the two memos.

options.text: The solver should print fewer numbers, so fewer of them get copied wrong
options.says: The fix is to stop copying, not to print less: each memo needs its numbers.

options.text: Both memos should be written by code from one stored record of the run
options.says: Right: one record holds the run's data, and each version formats it, so no number is typed by hand.

options.text: Each memo should get its own solve, so each group reads a fresh result
options.says: Two solves can return two plans; the versions must describe one run.

origin.section: One Record per Run, and Every Text Is Written From It

questions.stem: A finance note says a $2,000k budget cut lost $900k of NPV, 0.45 per $k. A director then plans a further $1,000k cut and books a $450k loss. What should the note have said about 0.45?

options.text: That it is the value of budget at the margin, good for any further cut
options.says: On a MILP the value of the next dollar is a step function; one average says nothing about the next cut.

options.text: That it is an average over that one cut, not the value of the next dollar
options.says: Right: the 0.415 in the lesson is labelled the same way; lessons 9.2.3 and 9.2.4 build the marginal curve.

options.text: That it is the budget row's shadow price, read from the MILP's solution
options.says: MathOpt returns no dual values for a MILP; the ratio came from two solves.

options.text: That it holds for cuts under $2,000k and doubles for any larger one
options.says: Nothing in one ratio predicts other cuts, smaller or larger; only more solves can.

origin.section: Finance Reads Money by Year, the Change in Value, and Whether It Is Proven

questions.stem: An auditor must confirm that a locked plan keeps every budget and alternative rule, even if a row was coded wrongly. Which evidence serves?

options.text: The model's own row slacks at the plan, since every kept row has slack of zero or more
options.says: A wrongly coded row would show slack too; the model agrees with its own mistakes.

options.text: The solver's OPTIMAL status, since a solver returns only plans that keep every row
options.says: It keeps the rows it was given; a wrong row is kept as faithfully as a right one.

options.text: A rerun of the same snapshot, since a repeated plan shows that the rows were right
options.says: A rerun repeats the same rows, wrong ones included; it is evidence about repeatability, not about the rows.

options.text: A check of the plan written from the input data, apart from the model's own rows
options.says: Right: verify reads the portfolio data and the plan, so a mistake in a row cannot hide in it.

origin.section: Auditors Read Inputs, Settings and Checks They Can Repeat Without the Model
